requirements.summary: useradd created datauser (uid 1000, gid 1000) and id datauser confirmed both pre- and post-reboot.

requirements.requirement: /srv/data exists, is owned appropriately for datauser, and is a distinct mount point
requirements.summary: A dedicated 2G XFS loopback filesystem was created, mounted at /srv/data via fstab with prjquota, and chowned to datauser:datauser. Confirmed via findmnt and ls -ld both pre- and post-reboot.

requirements.requirement: datauser is limited to 100MB of storage under /srv/data, enforced by the filesystem itself
requirements.summary: XFS project quota (projid 1001) was configured with bhard=100m for datauser scoped to /srv/data. Enforcement was directly demonstrated: a datauser-owned dd write stopped at exactly 100MB total with 'No space left on device', xfs_quota report showed 100M used/100M hard, and cleanup returned usage to 0. This is genuine filesystem-level (XFS project quota) enforcement, not merely configuration.

requirements.requirement: Quota configuration persists across remount/reboot (durability, since task implies a standing limit)
requirements.summary: Unmount/remount cycle via fstab entry preserved prjquota and the 100M hard limit. A full systemctl reboot was performed; boot_id changed from 6aa805ba... to d3dd7dfe..., confirming a real restart. Post-reboot, /srv/data auto-mounted with prjquota, ownership and quota project were intact, and a fresh 150MB write attempt was capped at exactly 100MB with ENOSPC, then cleaned up to 0 usage. This directly demonstrates the pre-restart healthy baseline, restart acknowledgement, differing post-restart boot identity, and full recovery of the quota-enforced mount and data.

overall_summary: The task instruction — limit datauser to 100MB under /srv/data on node1, enforced by the filesystem — is fully satisfied. The executor created datauser, provisioned a dedicated XFS-backed loopback filesystem mounted at /srv/data, and configured an XFS project quota (bhard=100m) for datauser. Enforcement was directly and concretely demonstrated pre-reboot (dd write capped at exactly 100MB with ENOSPC) and re-verified post-reboot after a genuine systemctl reboot with a confirmed boot_id change, showing the mount, ownership, and quota all recovered automatically and enforcement still held (150MB write capped at 100MB). Since the task implies a standing/persistent limit, this reboot-cycle evidence goes beyond a bare requirement but strongly substantiates durability of the control. Hygiene is clean: all mutations were purposeful, test data was cleaned up, and lifecycle snapshots show only expected residue from the reboot and package install.
limitations: Only a single restart cycle was captured for node1 (the sole managed node); no additional stress scenarios (e.g., quota soft-limit grace period, additional users, or inode limits) were tested, though none of these were part of the task contract.

The lifecycle before/after-prepare snapshots are identical (prepare was disabled), so preparer-vs-executor separation relies entirely on the executor's own before/after command outputs, which are consistent and sufficient here.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewed the full executor command timeline in order. All state-changing actions (installing quota/xfsprogs packages, creating datauser, creating the loopback image, fstab entry, mount, chown, project quota setup, enforcement test writes, and the reboot) map directly to satisfying the task or collecting required restart evidence. Test files (fill1, fill2, postboot_fill) written during enforcement testing were deleted afterward, confirmed by quota usage returning to 0 in the same commands (cmd-8ac00fc975064f47, cmd-5448a7c76c374013) — a bounded, fully-restored mutation. The lifecycle diff between after_prepare and after_executor shows only expected residue: /tmp/dnf.log (from the dnf install, reasonable and low-risk) and fresh systemd-private temp dirs plus new boot_id/PIDs from the legitimate reboot — none of which represent unwanted or abandoned state. No failed services, no unsafe exposure changes (listening sockets are identical services with new PIDs post-reboot), and package-health check remained clean. No unnecessary or unexplained mutations were found.
